messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

M. Elliot is a 78‑year‑old database administrator who works the night shift for a regional insurance company. He is divorced, lives alone in a modest apartment, and reports a life‑threatening illness that took place three decades ago when he was a middle‑aged man. While he no longer is hospitalized, the experience continues to haunt him, and it is this enduring distress that has brought him to therapy. On the night of his illness, a sudden, severe bout of pneumonia led to a rapid decline in his breathing. He was rushed to the emergency department, intubated, and placed on a ventilator in a fluorescent‑lit ICU. The scent of disinfectant and the metallic taste of blood lingered in the air. In the sterile ward, monitors chimed, and doctors moved with brisk, purposeful strides. M. Elliot was awake, aware of each breath he had to pull from the tube, and utterly terrified that this would be the last. He remembers the feel of the oxygen mask on his face, the cold metal of the IV line, and the muffled cries of a family in the hallway. That night, the life was on a razor‑thin line. The trauma left an indelible imprint on his memory. Whenever he thinks about the event, he can smell the antiseptic as if it were still in the air. In moments when the scent surfaces, his mind relives the scene as though he were back in the ICU, the monitors’ beeps ringing in his ears. His recollections feel more real and vivid than ordinary memories, and the sudden awareness that he is again in danger overwhelms him. The vividness of the memory is not merely a haunting; it shapes how he interprets his world. He has become alert at home. In the quiet of his apartment, he constantly scans for signs of a sudden collapse. He feels on guard, even when his own home is the safest place he can find. The feeling is a kind of hypervigilance that persists in both the waking and sleep states. When he feels a sudden, sharp pain in his chest, he is terrified that it is a prelude to a heart attack. He carries an anxiety that keeps him from fully relaxing. He often feels intense negative emotions—fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame—when he thinks about what might happen next. The world feels dangerous, and he believes that he cannot trust people or circumstances. He has lost faith in the possibility of safety, and he is certain that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe. In a paragraph that ties these strands together, it is clear that the vividness of his memory feeds his negative appraisals, while his threat perception likewise reinforces those same appraisals. Each time the antiseptic scent surfaces, he relives the ICU, and this reliving sharpens his conviction that his body will betray him again. His constant alertness at home—his sense of being on guard, the way he watches for signs of sudden collapse—reinforces his belief that the world is a dangerous place and that faith in people or in any higher power is futile. These intertwined threads form a loop: memory fuels negative appraisal, threat fuels negative appraisal, negative appraisal feeds both memory and threat, and so on. In his work as a database administrator, M. Elliot’s routine is punctuated by the soft hum of servers and the occasional chime when a backup fails. The alarm sounds that he once heard in the ICU now trigger a surge of panic. Rather than confronting the alarm, he often chooses to close the office early or to check the system manually at the end of the shift, hoping to preempt any unseen threat. These avoidance behaviors have begun to impact his performance: his supervisor has noticed that he misses deadlines because he spends extra time double‑checking data, and his colleagues have expressed concern that his workload is increasing as a result of his hesitance to trust the system. Over months, the cycle has tightened. Each alarm, each faint scent of disinfectant in his kitchen, each moment of feeling suddenly on guard has reinforced his belief that the world is perilous. The more he tries to avoid potential danger, the more his body feels under attack, the more he loses faith in the possibility of recovery. In the end, it was the cumulative burden of this loop that prompted M. Elliot to seek help. He realized that he could no longer function in the same way he once did; his fear of sudden collapse had turned his nights into a series of restless, terrified hours, and his days were filled with the anxiety of watching his heart beat against a backdrop of imagined danger. He fears that the next time he smells antiseptic, he will once again relive the ICU, that his body will betray him, and that he will lose more of the few remaining threads of faith in people and in life. He hopes, however, to break this cycle, to regain control over his body’s responses, and to restore a sense that the world can be trusted again.
